terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, intransitive; with an accusative, taste of something
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 2.6.104: occīsam saepe sapere plūs multō suem (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Said of the food, not of the person tasting, with an accusative of what it tastes of. To taste something oneself is gustāre.

phrases.english: Taste it. Do you like it?
This is not to my taste.
Have a little taste; maybe you’ll like it.

phrases.latin: sī colligere est nōn numquam dēcerpere ūvam, torculum invīsere, gustāre dē lacū mustum
phrases.english: if gathering means now and then picking a grape, looking in at the press, tasting the must from the vat

phrases.latin: Vāsō ahēneō neque nucleīs ad oleum nē ūtātur. Nam sī ūtētur, oleum male sapiet.
phrases.english: He is not to use a bronze vessel or the stones for the oil; for if he does, the oil will taste bad.

phrases.latin: nec dubium quīn fīcī rāmulīs glaciātus cāseus jūcundissimē sapiat
phrases.english: and there is no doubt that cheese curdled with fig twigs tastes best of all

phrases.latin: ego contrā plūs lībram comēdī, nam ipsum aprum sapiēbat
phrases.english: I, on the other hand, ate more than a pound, because it tasted just like wild boar

sources: Lewis & Short: gusto · Lewis & Short: placeo
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 59, 73.
Lewis & Short: sapio
